Field surveys of the Longsnout boarfish (Pentaceropsis recurvirostris) along the temperate reefs of southern Australia have provided detailed life-history information for this endemic species. Examination of gonadal tissue from a large sample of reproductively active individuals revealed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 9.8% [GSI = 9.8%], based on specimens collected at a water temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]. This relatively high index, compared to other members of the Pentacerotidae, suggests a concentrated investment in gamete production characteristic of batch-spawning fishes. In terms of body size composition, the maximum total length recorded across all sampled populations was 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a value that likely represents the asymptotic size approached by older individuals in this species. This ultimate length is consistent with previously published maximum sizes for the genus and provides a useful benchmark for growth curve estimation in future population dynamics studies.

Reproductive development in Pentaceropsis recurvirostris follows a pattern typical of many temperate marine teleosts, with a clear size threshold marking the transition to maturity. The total length at which 50% of individuals reach puberty is 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters], a metric derived from microscopic examination of gonadal histology across a wide size range of specimens. This length-at-puberty corresponds closely to the onset of active gametogenesis and is notably smaller than the ultimate length, indicating a substantial post-puberty growth phase. At the onset of maturity, the average wet weight at puberty was calculated to be 284.7 grams [Wwp = 284.7 grams], based on the length-weight relationship established for this species. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males, estimated from the same allometric equation applied to the maximum length, reaches 2600 grams [Wwi = 2600 grams], highlighting the considerable scope for somatic growth remaining after reproductive activity begins.

Embryonic and early larval development in the Longsnout boarfish proceed rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions that simulate natural thermal regimes. Hatching was observed to occur after approximately 4.9 days [ab = approximately 4.9 days] when the incubation medium was maintained at a stable temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C], a duration that aligns well with predictions from general teleost egg-development models at this thermal level. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is still completely dependent on its endogenous reserves, and at this stage it possesses a very small initial structural mass. The estimated wet weight at birth, computed from the mean egg dimensions of 1.1 millimeters in length and 0.6 millimeters in width, is 0.00021 grams [Wwb = 0.00021 grams], a value that reflects the modest amount of yolk provisioned into each fertilized ovum. This tiny birth mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among inshore marine fishes of similar adult body size.

Longevity records derived from otolith-based age estimation for wild-caught specimens indicate that the lifespan of Pentaceropsis recurvirostris is quite extended for a fish of its body size. The maximum documented lifespan, obtained from individuals inhabiting cooler waters, was calculated to be just over 55 years [am = just over 55 years] based on daily ring counts validated with marginal increment analysis, all recorded at an ambient temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C]. This exceptionally long life span, comparable to some deep-water or high-latitude species, suggests a slow-paced life-history strategy with delayed senescence. Such a prolonged adult phase is consistent with the species' low natural mortality rate and its position as a relatively large-bodied predator in the reef community. The longevity estimate also has important implications for the species' vulnerability to fishing pressure, as populations with long-lived individuals require many years to recover from over-exploitation.

The overall life-history syndrome of the Longsnout boarfish combines relatively slow growth with a late onset of maturation and a remarkably long reproductive lifespan. Individuals first attain puberty at 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters] in total length, a size that is reached after several years of juvenile growth, and they may continue to spawn annually for multiple decades thereafter. The maximum length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] is achieved only by the oldest fish in the population. Ecologically, this fish occupies a demersal niche on continental shelf reefs, where it forages on benthic invertebrates. The gonadosomatic index was 9.8% [GSI = 9.8%], and the life span extends to 55 years [am = 55 years] at a temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C] at a temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C].
